summary:
HyperBlink is a web tool that lets anyone see how the infrared sky changes, using NASA SPHEREx data. Type the name or coordinates of any object. HyperBlink finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, aligns them on one north-up grid, stacks each visit and plays them as a flipbook, so moving stars, brown dwarfs and variable stars stand out. Click any point to see its spectrum across 102 bands, visit by visit.

The challenge asks for a public-facing way to see the time-variable sky. Today that takes archive tools, multi-extension FITS files and Python. HyperBlink needs no account, no download and no code, and it teaches as you go with a built-in guide and glossary.

It matters because blinking survey images is how Backyard Worlds volunteers found real brown dwarfs, some of the Sun’s nearest neighbours, in NASA’s WISE data. HyperBlink brings that to SPHEREx and works as an on-ramp to NASA/IPAC IRSA.
details:
What it does

- Search by name or coordinates in either format, or open one of the five challenge targets, which load at once from a pre-built snapshot.

- Names resolve to where the object is today: the catalogue position is moved along its proper motion. For a fast mover like WISE 0855, that’s a difference of about 2′.

- Every exposure is aligned on one north-up grid and each visit is stacked. The frames play as a blink on one shared grey scale, so a change in brightness between frames is real.

- Switch between the six detectors (0.75 to 5 µm), or see them as six tiles side by side or a three-detector colour view.

- Difference images show only what changed. Shift-and-add stacks frames along a proper motion so a faint mover adds up in one place.

- Click any point to measure its spectrum across 102 bands, one line per visit, with a CSV download. Saturated points are flagged and drawn hollow.

- Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 overlays are moved to each visit’s date, with links to SIMBAD and VizieR.

- The whole view is stored in the URL, so a link reopens it exactly. An /embed route serves iframes. An all-sky SPHEREx map lets you pick a field by clicking.

How it works

1. Look up the name with CDS Sesame and move it to today by its proper motion.

2. Find every SPHEREx Level 2 exposure through IRSA’s image search (SIA).

3. Read only the needed pixel rows from IRSA’s public Amazon S3 mirror.

4. Reproject each exposure to north-up with Astropy and reproject.

5. Stack each visit on a shared scale.

Spectra come from forced photometry across all 102 bands. New data releases are found automatically, a freshness badge shows how recent the data is, and one script rebuilds the featured snapshot.

Benefits and impact

- Public, students and teachers: see a star move in seconds and learn what they’re looking at along the way.

- Citizen scientists: the Backyard Worlds workflow (blink, spot, check), now with SPHEREx data.

- Astronomers: a quick look and a link to share before opening IRSA’s full tools.

The intended impact is more people looking at SPHEREx data, and more eyes on the moving and changing sky.

Tools and languages

- API: Python with FastAPI, Astropy, reproject and NumPy.

- Web app: TypeScript with Next.js and React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, and Aladin Lite for the sky map.

- Monorepo: Turborepo and pnpm.

- Hardware: none.

Creativity

- It pairs a blink with a spectrum for every visit, so one tool covers both motion and colour.

- Names resolve to where the object is now, not where the catalogue says it was.

- Catalogue overlays move with each frame’s date.

- The demo payoff: WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is barely visible in the images, but its spectrum climbs from 4 to 5 µm, its signature, in a few clicks.

Factors we considered

- Newcomers first: sensible defaults (asinh stretch, outlier clipping, a 4′ field, the detector where the target is brightest), plain language, and help shown beside the viewer.

- Scientific honesty:

- one shared grey scale for all frames;

- flagged pixels shown as no data;

- relative fluxes only, with no aperture correction;

- limits stated plainly: 6.15″ pixels, and only one to one and a half years between the first and last visits.

- Speed: the first view of a new field takes about a minute, repeat views are cached, and the featured targets are pre-built.

- Updates: new releases are discovered automatically.

- Credit: HyperBlink is an on-ramp to IRSA, not a replacement, and every pixel comes from IRSA.
